上低音號主要出現在銅管樂團、軍樂隊與管樂團中。在英國銅管樂團裡，它常以高音譜號記: The euphonium appears mainly in brass bands, military bands and wind bands. In British brass bands it is often written in treble clef and takes the tenor and baritone parts; American wind bands may use either treble or bass clef. In the mid-nineteenth century the saxhorn was popular in British and American bands and was promoted by the Distin family, becoming an important voice of the British brass band movement. Its forebears and related instruments were also found in France, in British military bands, in orchestras and in civic brass bands.
上低音號的歷史與低音號及閥鍵銅管發展相連。1817年Asté製出ophiclei: The history of the euphonium is bound up with the ophicleide and with the development of valved brass. In 1817 Asté made the ophicleide, whose wide conical bore gave a warm tone; in the 1830s and 40s Vienna added valves to the ophicleide, producing the bombardon. In 1843 Sommer developed the Sommerophone and took out a patent on it the following year under the name Euphonion, and after the 1851 Great Exhibition in London the name reached Britain. Sax's saxhorn basse was another early modern form, promoted in Britain and America by the Distin family; Červený's Baroxyton of 1852 and the later Kaiserbaryton became the common pattern in east-central Europe.

It sounds by way of the lips buzzing in the mouthpiece, and its wide conical bore gives it a warm, solemn timbre. Compared with the British tenor horn of the same family, that instrument has a narrower bore, a smaller bell and often lacks the fourth valve; compared with the American baritone horn, that one has a narrower bore and a bell that curves forward. 上低音號（Euphonium）屬唇振氣鳴／號角與銅管，H-S 編號 423.23: The euphonium is a lip-reed aerophone of the horn and brass group, H-S number 423.232, a valved brass instrument in B-flat, an octave below the B-flat trumpet. The player sounds it by buzzing the lips in the mouthpiece; the instrument has a wide conical bore, most examples carry four compensating piston valves, and four or five rotary valves are also common in eastern and central Europe. With the tuba and its relatives it belongs to the family of valved horns, and it is used mainly in brass bands, military bands and concert wind bands.
